en.title: French: the whole course
en.short: What French studies covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: French is the study of the French language, its linguistics, literature and the cultures of France and the French-speaking world. It is not only learning to speak. You study how the language is built, how it changes, how it is used in society, and what its writers have made with it. The French-speaking world includes France, parts of Belgium, Switzerland and Canada, the Caribbean, the Maghreb and many countries in West and Central Africa. French is an official language in many African states. The notes are in English. French words appear only where spelling is certain, including accents.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a B.A. French is commonly a four-year degree, but combined honours, direct entry and year-abroad arrangements vary. The National Universities Commission (NUC) oversees university programmes; check your own handbook for the exact structure. Some Nigerian programmes include a period of language immersion, often at the Nigerian French Language Village, or teaching practice. In France, the Licence in languages and literatures usually takes three years, followed by a two-year Master. In the United Kingdom, a BA French often takes three or four years, with the four-year version including a year abroad. Polytechnics and colleges may offer diplomas with different lengths. Always confirm the current rules, credit loads and graduation requirements with your department.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Early topics build the base. You start with the sounds of French and the International Phonetic Alphabet, then grammar: gender, articles and the simple sentence. You study verb conjugation groups and core tenses, vocabulary and word formation, listening and spoken French, reading strategies, writing with correct spelling and accents, and dictionary and reference skills. An introduction to France and the French-speaking world sets the context.

Core work goes deeper. Advanced grammar and syntax, phonetics and phonology, morphology and lexicology, semantics and pragmatics, and sociolinguistics and the francophone world study the language as a system and as a social fact. The history of French explains how the language developed. Literary analysis and explication de texte teach close reading. Literature courses cover the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the nineteenth century, and the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Francophone African literature and Caribbean and Maghrebian literature widen the canon. Civilisation and institutions, and society and culture in francophone Africa, study how people live and how states work. Translation theory and practice, teaching French as a foreign language, and research methods prepare you for professional and academic work.

At master’s level, advanced linguistic theory, literary theory and criticism, postcolonial and francophone studies, and dissertation research and writing become central.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study a little every day. Language learning rewards regular contact more than last-minute cramming. Listen to French radio, podcasts or films, and repeat aloud. Keep a vocabulary notebook with words in sentences, not isolated lists. Learn the International Phonetic Alphabet early; it helps you check pronunciation in a dictionary. Write short paragraphs and ask someone to correct them. Keep an error log of your repeated mistakes.

For literature, read the set text before the lecture. Note the structure, the main themes, the historical setting and two or three stylistic devices. For linguistics, define each term and give a French example. For civilisation, name the country and the institution, and check official sources because laws and institutions change. Use a good bilingual dictionary and a grammar reference; do not rely on machine translation for submitted work.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is to ignore accents and spelling. Accents change meaning and are part of correct French. Another is to translate English word for word. French word order, pronouns and tenses often differ. Students also treat grammatical gender as natural gender; it is a property of nouns. Some learn verb forms by rote without seeing the pattern, so they cannot use a new verb.

In literature, students summarise the plot and forget to analyse how the text works. In civilisation, they present one country’s practice as universal. In linguistics, they give an English example and call it French. In research, they use a sample that cannot support the claim. Finally, many rely on machine translation and do not check the result.

keyPoints: French studies the language, linguistics, literature and cultures of France and the French-speaking world.
Degree length and awards differ by country; check your own programme handbook.
Start with sounds, grammar and verbs, then move to linguistics, literature, civilisation, translation and research.
Practise listening, speaking, reading and writing every day, and keep an error log.
Accents and spelling are part of meaning; do not ignore them.
Name the country when discussing institutions, laws or varieties of French.

en.title: The Sounds of French and the International Phonetic Alphabet
en.short: French vowels, nasals, consonants, rhythm, liaison, elision and reading IPA.

sections.heading: Vowels and nasals
sections.text: French vowels are front or back, rounded or unrounded, and oral or nasal. The four traditional nasal vowels are /ɑ̃/ as in banc, /ɛ̃/ as in vin, /ɔ̃/ as in bon, and /œ̃/ as in brun. Many speakers now pronounce /œ̃/ like /ɛ̃/, so dictionaries may show one or two symbols. The oral vowels include /i y u/, /e ø o/, /ɛ œ ɔ/, and /a/. The symbol /ə/ is the schwa, the weak vowel heard in le when it is not elided. Do not trust spelling: eau, au and ô can all be /o/.

sections.heading: Consonants and syllables
sections.text: French consonants are described by place, manner and voicing. /p b/ are bilabial stops, /t d/ alveolar stops, /k ɡ/ velar stops. /f v s z ʃ ʒ/ are fricatives. /m n ɲ/ are nasals. /l/ and /ʁ/ are liquids; French r is usually uvular, not the English r. French has no /h/ sound in native words. Syllables usually begin with a consonant: a.mi, not am.i. A final consonant is often silent unless a vowel follows in liaison. In les amis, the s of les becomes /z/: /le.z‿a.mi/. Elision drops a vowel before another vowel: le ami becomes l’ami.

sections.heading: Stress, rhythm and IPA
sections.text: French stress falls on the last syllable of a rhythmic group, a phrase spoken as one unit, not on every word. This gives French its even rhythm. Read the IPA chart by rows and columns: consonant rows show manner, columns show place, and paired symbols show voiceless and voiced sounds. On the vowel chart, height, backness and lip rounding locate each vowel. Use minimal pairs in ear training: tu /ty/ against tout /tu/, dessus /də.sy/ against dessous /də.su/. For production, say the pair aloud, record yourself, and compare with a model. Take a spelling such as oiseaux /wa.zo/: seven letters, two syllables, the s gives the /z/, and the final x is silent. Check each symbol in a dictionary.

keyPoints: French has four traditional nasal vowels /ɑ̃/, /ɛ̃/, /ɔ̃/ and /œ̃/, though /œ̃/ merges with /ɛ̃/ for many speakers.
French consonants are classified by place, manner and voicing, and French r is usually /ʁ/.
Stress falls on the final syllable of a rhythmic group, not on every word.
Liaison pronounces a normally silent final consonant before a vowel, as in les amis /le.z‿a.mi/.
Elision drops a vowel before another vowel, as in l’ami.
The IPA chart shows consonants by place and manner and vowels by height, backness and rounding; use minimal pairs for ear training.

en.title: French Grammar: Gender, Articles and the Simple Sentence
en.short: Gender, articles, adjective agreement, pronouns, negation and three ways to ask questions.

sections.heading: Gender and articles
sections.text:
Every French noun has a grammatical gender, masculine or feminine. Gender belongs to the word, not always to the thing: le livre (book) is masculine, la table is feminine. Learn each noun with its article and check a dictionary for m or f.

The definite article means the: le, la, l’ before a vowel or silent h, les. The indefinite article means a or an: un, une, des. The partitive article means some or an unspecified amount: du, de la, de l’, des. Examples: le pain, un pain, du pain; la soupe, une soupe, de la soupe; des légumes.

sections.heading: Adjectives and pronouns
sections.text: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number: un petit garçon, une petite fille, des petits garçons. Most adjectives follow the noun: une voiture rouge. A few common short adjectives usually come before it: petit, grand, jeune, beau, bon, mauvais, nouveau. Subject pronouns are je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. On often means one or people in general, and in everyday speech it usually means we; it takes the third-person singular verb.

sections.heading: Negation and questions
sections.text:
Negation wraps the verb: ne + verb + pas. Je ne parle pas anglais. In speech, ne is often dropped: Je parle pas anglais. After a negative, an indefinite or partitive article usually becomes de or d’: Je n’ai pas de pain; Elle ne boit pas d’eau. The definite article stays: Je n’aime pas le café.

There are three basic ways to ask a yes-no question. Intonation: Tu parles français ? Est-ce que: Est-ce que tu parles français ? Inversion: Parles-tu français ? Inversion is formal; intonation is common in speech.

sections.heading: Building sentences
sections.text: A simple sentence needs a subject and a verb, and may add a complement: La petite fille mange une pomme verte. La petite fille is feminine singular, so petite ends in e. The verb mange agrees with the subject. Pomme is feminine, so verte also ends in e. Find the verb, then the subject, then check every adjective against its noun.

keyPoints: French nouns are masculine or feminine, and the gender is best learned with the article.
Definite articles are le, la, l’ and les; indefinite are un, une and des; partitive are du, de la, de l’ and des.
Adjectives agree in gender and number, and most follow the noun.
Subject pronouns are je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils and elles.
Negation is ne + verb + pas, and indefinite or partitive articles become de after a negative.
Ask yes-no questions by intonation, est-ce que or inversion.

en.title: French Verbs: Conjugation Groups and Core Tenses
en.short: Conjugation groups, regular and irregular verbs, six core tenses, auxiliaries, agreement, reflexives and imperative.

sections.heading: Three groups
sections.text: French grammar divides verbs into three groups. Group one is regular verbs ending in -er, except aller: parler gives je parle, nous parlons. Group two is regular -ir verbs that add -iss- in the plural: finir gives je finis, nous finissons. Group three holds all other verbs, mainly -re and -oir verbs and irregular -ir verbs such as partir. Aller is irregular. Common irregulars include être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir, venir and prendre.

sections.heading: Present and future
sections.text: The present tense states facts, habits and current actions: je travaille. The near future (futur proche) is aller in the present plus an infinitive: je vais partir. It suits immediate plans. The simple future (futur simple) adds -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive: je parlerai, nous parlerons. Verbs ending in -re drop the final e. Irregular stems include être ser-, avoir aur-, aller ir-, faire fer- and pouvoir pourr-.

sections.heading: Past tenses
sections.text: The imperfect (imparfait) describes background, habits and ongoing states. Its stem is the nous form of the present minus -ons, plus -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient: nous parlons gives je parlais. The compound past (passé composé) is the present of avoir or être plus a past participle: j’ai parlé, elle est allée. It reports a completed action. The pluperfect (plus-que-parfait) uses the imperfect of the auxiliary plus the participle: j’avais parlé. It marks an action completed before another past action.

sections.heading: Auxiliary and agreement
sections.text: Avoir is the default auxiliary. Être is used with pronominal verbs and a small set of intransitive verbs of motion or change, such as aller, venir, arriver and partir. With être the participle agrees with the subject: elle est allée. With avoir it agrees only with a preceding direct object: les lettres que j’ai écrites. Reflexive verbs take a pronoun: je me lève; je me suis levé(e). The imperative drops the subject: Parle ! Finis ! Lève-toi !

keyPoints: First-group verbs end in -er and are regular except aller; second-group verbs are regular -ir verbs with -iss- in the plural.
The near future is aller in the present plus an infinitive; the simple future adds -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive.
The imperfect stem comes from the nous form of the present minus -ons.
The compound past is the present of avoir or être plus a past participle; the pluperfect uses the imperfect of the auxiliary.
With être the participle agrees with the subject; with avoir it agrees only with a preceding direct object.
Reflexive verbs use a pronoun and take être in the compound past; the imperative drops the subject pronoun.

en.title: Vocabulary Building and Word Formation in French
en.short: How French words are built, how register and collocation work, and how to learn vocabulary.

sections.heading: Building words
sections.text: A word can be divided into a root and affixes. A prefix goes before the root and often changes meaning: faire (to do), refaire (to do again), défaire (to undo). A suffix goes after the root and often changes word class: rapide (quick) gives rapidement (quickly); chanter (to sing) gives chanteur (singer). A word family is a group of words sharing a root, such as chant, chanson, chanter and chanteur. Learn the family, not only one word.

sections.heading: Compounding and conversion
sections.text: Compounding joins two or more words into one meaning: porte-monnaie (purse), arc-en-ciel (rainbow). Conversion uses one form in a new word class without adding an affix: le dîner (dinner, noun) and dîner (to dine, verb); le sourire (smile, noun) and sourire (to smile, verb). Notice the article: it often shows the noun.

sections.heading: Register and collocation
sections.text: Register is the level of formality of a word. Voiture (car) is neutral, bagnole is informal, and automobile is formal. Collocation means words that habitually go together. French says prendre une décision (to make a decision), not faire une décision, and commettre une erreur (to make a mistake). Store each new word in a short phrase, with its gender and register.

sections.heading: Cognates and learning
sections.text: Cognates look similar in English and French: table, nation. False friends look similar but differ: librairie means bookshop, not library; actuel means current, not actual; assister à means to attend, not to assist. Check a dictionary before trusting a guess. Learn vocabulary by grouping word families, learning collocations, and using spaced repetition: review a word after one day, then three days, then a week. A student who meets librairie in a text may guess library; the dictionary corrects it to bookshop.

keyPoints: A prefix comes before the root and often changes meaning; a suffix comes after it and often changes word class.
A word family groups words that share a root, such as chant, chanson, chanter and chanteur.
Compounding joins words, while conversion changes word class without adding an affix.
Register is the level of formality; collocation is the habit of words to occur together.
Cognates look alike in English and French, but false friends such as librairie and actuel do not mean what they seem.
Learn each word with its gender, a short phrase, its register and its family, and review it at spaced intervals.

en.title: Listening Comprehension and Spoken French
en.short: Understanding fast spoken French, numbers and transactions, and speaking with tu and vous.

sections.heading: Hearing natural speed
sections.text: Natural French is not a string of separate words. In connected speech, words run together, and common expressions are reduced. In informal speech the ne of negation is often dropped: je ne sais pas becomes je sais pas. Tu as may sound like t’as, and il y a like y a. Do not copy these forms in a formal exam until you know the register, the level of formality. Listen for the stressed final syllable. If you miss a word, keep listening and use the situation. Ask: Pouvez-vous répéter, s’il vous plaît ?

sections.heading: Numbers, dates and times
sections.text: Numbers decide many transactions. Prices use a comma: 3,50 € is trois euros cinquante. Two items at 3,50 € and 4,20 € total 3,50 + 4,20 = 7,70 €, or sept euros soixante-dix. Dates use le plus a number: le 3 mai; the first is le premier mai. Timetables often use the 24-hour clock: 15:30 is quinze heures trente. For an appointment say J’ai rendez-vous à quinze heures trente. Repeat the number back to confirm.

sections.heading: Everyday transactions
sections.text: In a shop, Combien ça coûte ? asks the price, and Je voudrais... is a polite way to ask for something. For travel, Un billet pour..., s’il vous plaît is a safe pattern. For appointments, Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous and J’ai rendez-vous à... are useful. Listen for the other person’s question before answering. A short case: Amina wants a ticket to Abidjan for Tuesday at 8 a.m. She hears Un billet pour Abidjan, mardi à huit heures ? and confirms Oui, c’est ça. Repeating key details checks date, time and destination.

sections.heading: Speaking and register
sections.text: Use bonjour in most daytime greetings and bonsoir in the evening; salut is informal. Je m’appelle... introduces you, and Je viens du Nigeria states origin. Use vous with strangers, older people and formal situations. Use tu with friends, family, children and peers in informal settings; workplace norms vary by country and generation. When unsure, choose vous. For a short talk, give a clear opening, then signpost with d’abord, ensuite and enfin. Describe, give one example, and close politely.

keyPoints: In connected speech, words run together and common forms are reduced; informal French often drops ne.
Prices use a comma and dates use le plus a number; timetables often use the 24-hour clock.
Polite transaction patterns include Je voudrais..., Combien ça coûte ? and Un billet pour..., s’il vous plaît.
Use vous with strangers and formal contacts; use tu with friends, family and children, but norms vary.
Ask for repetition with Pouvez-vous répéter, s’il vous plaît ? and repeat key details to confirm.
A short talk needs a clear opening, signposts such as d’abord, ensuite and enfin, and a close.

en.title: Reading French: Comprehension Strategies
en.short: Skimming, scanning, context clues, connectors, tense markers and telling text types apart in French.

sections.heading: Skim and scan
sections.text: Skimming means reading quickly for the main idea: title, first lines, repeated words. Scanning means looking for one detail, such as a date, price or name. In a notice, scan for the verb and the time. In a news item, skim the first paragraph, because French news writing often puts the main fact there. Then read sentence by sentence, asking who does what. Do not stop at every unknown word.

sections.heading: Guess from context
sections.text: Guess meaning from context before using a dictionary. Ask what word class fits the gap and what the sentence already says. In “Le train part à huit heures, donc nous devons partir tôt”, donc signals a result. If part is unknown, the time phrase and donc show departure. Check guesses against the next sentence. A word may look like English but differ, so confirm from use.

sections.heading: Connectors and time
sections.text: Connectors show how ideas join. Addition: et, aussi. Contrast: mais, cependant. Cause: parce que, car. Result: donc. Time: d’abord, ensuite, enfin. Tense markers place events: hier, aujourd’hui, demain, and verb endings. You need not conjugate here; notice whether the passage looks back, describes now, or predicts. In a letter, cher or chère and the closing formula help identify the writer and reader.

sections.heading: Text types
sections.text: Narrative passages tell events in time, often with past tenses and time connectors. Descriptive passages paint a scene, with adjectives and present tense. Argumentative passages defend a view, with connectors of cause, contrast and conclusion. A literary extract may mix all three. Practice with a short letter: skim for the writer’s purpose, scan for names and dates, then mark connectors and tense markers. Summarise each paragraph in one English sentence.

keyPoints: Skim for the main idea and scan for one detail; do not read every word equally.
Guess unknown words from sentence context and confirm the guess in the next sentence.
Connectors such as mais, donc and parce que show contrast, result and cause.
Tense markers and time words show whether a passage looks back, describes now or predicts.
Narrative, descriptive and argumentative passages have different signals and can mix in one text.
Summarise each paragraph in one English sentence to check comprehension.

en.title: Writing French: Spelling, Accents and Paragraphs
en.short: French spelling and accents, punctuation, paragraph linking, and informal and semi-formal writing.

sections.heading: Accents and spelling
sections.text: French spelling is partly historical: letters once pronounced may now be silent, so learners memorise word forms. The five accents are the aigu (é), grave (è), circonflexe (ê), cédille (ç) and tréma (ë). The aigu closes e; the grave opens it and distinguishes words such as ou (or) and où (where). The circonflexe often marks an old s, as in hôtel. The cédille keeps c soft before a, o, u: ça, garçon, reçu. The tréma separates vowels: Noël, naïve. Accents change meaning: a (has) and à (to); sur (on) and sûr (sure).

sections.heading: Punctuation and paragraphs
sections.text: French punctuation follows conventions that differ from English. Put a space before ; : ! ? and inside guillemets « », but not before a comma or full stop. Use « » for quotations, with a space after the opening mark and before the closing mark. A paragraph develops one idea. Begin with a topic sentence, support it, then link to the next. Useful connectors are d’abord, ensuite, enfin for order; cependant and pourtant for contrast; donc and par conséquent for result; par exemple for illustration. Avoid stringing short sentences without links.

sections.heading: Messages and letters
sections.text: Informal messages use tu with a known friend; semi-formal letters use vous. A short message states the purpose, gives the needed detail and closes. A letter has a greeting, body and closing formula. In a narration, use past tenses consistently and time markers: d’abord, puis, ensuite, finalement. In description, place adjectives after nouns usually and make them agree. Check every accent, verb ending and plural before sending.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Learners often drop accents, confuse homophones (ses, ces, c’est; leur, leurs), and forget agreement. They also copy English punctuation or word order. A useful check is to read aloud, then verify accents and endings. Example: 'Jai recu ton message, je suis tres content.' Correct: 'J’ai reçu ton message ; je suis très content.' The apostrophe, cédille and accents are required.

keyPoints: French uses five accent marks: aigu, grave, circonflexe, cédille and tréma.
Accents and cedillas change pronunciation and meaning, so never omit them.
French punctuation puts a space before ; : ! ? and inside guillemets « ».
A paragraph should develop one idea and use connectors such as d’abord, cependant and donc.
Informal messages use tu; semi-formal letters use vous and a closing formula.
Check homophones, verb endings, plurals and accents before sending any text.

en.title: Dictionaries, Grammar References and How to Learn a Language
en.short: How to read French dictionary entries, use grammar references and learn vocabulary and grammar effectively.

sections.heading: Dictionary entries
sections.text: A bilingual dictionary gives French and English equivalents; a monolingual French dictionary defines French words in French. In an entry, find the headword (the word listed), then the pronunciation, part of speech and gender. Labels include n.m. (nom masculin), n.f. (nom féminin), adj. (adjectif), v. (verbe), fig. (figuré, figurative) and fam. (familier, informal). Read the examples: they show collocations (usual word pairs) and register (level of formality). For instance, maison is n.f., with examples such as une maison de campagne. Check the abbreviation list.

sections.heading: Grammar references
sections.text: Grammar references explain rules and patterns; verb tables list forms. Standard works include Le Bon Usage by Maurice Grevisse and the Bescherelle verb tables. Use the index to find a point, read the examples, then write your own sentence. Online, the CNRTL (a free French language resource site) and its TLFi dictionary are reliable for French usage. Publisher sites such as Larousse and Le Robert are useful, but check what kind of page it is. Cross-check a doubtful point in two sources.

sections.heading: Learning vocabulary
sections.text: Learn vocabulary in context, not as isolated lists. Record a word with its gender, a short phrase and its register. Learn frequent words and chunks (common word groups) first; they appear most often. Use spaced repetition: review after one day, three days, a week, then longer gaps. Say or write the word from memory before checking. For grammar, learn a pattern with two or three examples, then produce new sentences. Keep errors in a log and revisit them.

sections.heading: Revising and testing
sections.text: Revise little and often. Test yourself by covering the translation or definition and recalling it; this is retrieval practice, and it is more effective than rereading. Mix old and new items. Use the dictionary to check gender, spelling and register when you write. A simple weekly cycle is: learn ten items, test them after a day, use them in five sentences, then review after a week. If a test shows a gap, return to the example, not just the rule.

keyPoints: A dictionary entry gives the headword, pronunciation, part of speech, gender, labels and examples.
Learn the abbreviation list: n.m. and n.f. show masculine and feminine nouns, adj. and v. give other parts of speech, and fig. and fam. mark figurative and informal uses.
Use grammar references and verb tables to check patterns, then write your own examples.
Reliable online sources include the CNRTL and its TLFi; cross-check doubtful points in two sources.
Learn vocabulary in context with gender and phrases, using spaced repetition and retrieval practice.
Test yourself by recall, not rereading, and correct errors by returning to examples.

en.title: An Introduction to France and the French-Speaking World
en.short: A first map of France, la francophonie, French-speaking countries and basic institutions.

sections.heading: What la francophonie means
sections.text: La francophonie means the French-speaking world. It includes people who speak French as a first, second or foreign language. The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) is a political and cultural organisation of member states, not a list of all French speakers. French has different statuses: official language, co-official language, administrative language, or a widely taught second language. A country can be French-speaking without making French official.

sections.heading: France and its regions
sections.text: France is a unitary republic. Since the 2016 regional reform, metropolitan France has 13 administrative regions. Five overseas departments are Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion and Mayotte. They are part of France and, as outermost regions, part of the European Union. Overseas collectivities such as French Polynesia, Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon and Wallis-et-Futuna have their own statuses and more autonomy. New Caledonia is separate again, with a special status of its own. French is the official language throughout the Republic; local languages are also spoken but are not official.

sections.heading: Countries and capitals
sections.text: Examples show the range. In Africa, Senegal (Dakar) has French as official language; Côte d’Ivoire (Yamoussoukro) has French official; Cameroon (Yaoundé) has French and English official; the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kinshasa) has French official. In the Caribbean, Haiti (Port-au-Prince) has Haitian Creole and French official. In North America, Canada (Ottawa) has English and French official at federal level, and Quebec has French as its official language. In Europe, Belgium (Brussels) has Dutch, French and German official; Switzerland (Bern, the federal city) has French as a national and official language.

sections.heading: Institutions and daily life
sections.text: France is a semi-presidential republic under the 1958 Constitution. The directly elected president appoints the prime minister; the government is responsible to the National Assembly. Parliament has the National Assembly and the Senate. Local government runs through communes, departments and regions. The state is secular (laïcité). French is the language of administration and school. The euro is used in metropolitan France and the overseas departments; some Pacific collectivities use the CFP franc. Rules and rates change, so check current official sources.

keyPoints: La francophonie is the French-speaking world; the OIF is an organisation of member states, not all French speakers.
France is a unitary republic with 13 metropolitan regions and five overseas departments.
Overseas collectivities have their own statuses and more autonomy than overseas departments; New Caledonia has a separate special status.
French has official, co-official or administrative status in different countries; some French-speaking countries do not make it official.

Examples include Senegal (Dakar), Côte d’Ivoire (Yamoussoukro), Cameroon (Yaoundé), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kinshasa), Haiti (Port-au-Prince), Canada (Ottawa), Belgium (Brussels) and Switzerland (Bern, the federal city).
France’s Fifth Republic Constitution dates from 1958; the president is directly elected and the government is responsible to the National Assembly.

en.title: Advanced French Grammar and Syntax
en.short: The full verb system, complex clauses, pronouns, passive and impersonal forms, and sentence analysis.

sections.heading: The verb system
sections.text: The subjunctive is a mood for doubt, wish, emotion and necessity: Je doute qu’il vienne. The conditional expresses hypothesis, politeness and future-in-the-past: S’il pleuvait, je resterais. Literary tenses, mainly written, include the passé simple, the imparfait du subjonctif, the plus-que-parfait du subjonctif and the passé antérieur. In reported speech after a past verb, French usually shifts tenses: present to imperfect, passé composé to plus-que-parfait, future to conditional. Il a dit qu’il viendrait. A fact still true may stay in the present.

sections.heading: Complex sentences
sections.text: A complex sentence has a main clause and one or more subordinate clauses. A relative clause modifies a noun: L’homme qui parle est mon frère. A complement clause fills a verb’s object: Je pense qu’il viendra. A concessive clause concedes a difficulty: Bien qu’il pleuve, nous sortons. Même s’il pleut, nous sortons uses the indicative. Learn the conjunction and the mood it requires.

sections.heading: Pronouns and voice
sections.text: The pronoun y replaces à plus a thing or place: Je pense à Paris, j’y pense. En replaces de plus a noun or quantity: Il a des livres, il en a. Relative pronouns are qui for subject, que for object, dont for de, and où for place or time. Demonstrative pronouns are celui, celle, ceux, celles, ceci and cela. The passive uses être plus past participle, with the agent usually introduced by par: La porte est ouverte par le gardien. Impersonal and indefinite constructions use il or on: Il faut partir; On parle français ici.

sections.heading: Analysis and errors
sections.text: To analyse a sentence, find the main subject and verb, then mark each clause and its function. Check agreement. With être, the past participle agrees with the subject: Les lettres sont parties. With avoir, it agrees with a preceding direct object: Les lettres qu’il a écrites sont parties. Common errors include using the indicative after bien que, forgetting the subjunctive after il faut que, and overusing literary tenses in speech. Read the whole sentence before correcting.

keyPoints: The subjunctive is used after expressions of doubt, wish, emotion, necessity and after conjunctions such as bien que and pour que.
The conditional covers hypothesis, politeness and future-in-the-past, and si plus the imperfect takes the conditional present.
Literary tenses such as the passé simple and the imparfait du subjonctif belong mainly to written narrative.
In reported speech after a past verb, present shifts to imperfect, passé composé to plus-que-parfait, and future to conditional.
Y replaces à plus a thing or place, en replaces de plus a noun or quantity, and qui, que, dont and où are relative pronouns.
The passive is être plus past participle, often with par, and impersonal and indefinite constructions use il or on; check participle agreement.

en.title: French Phonetics and Phonology: System and Variation
en.short: French phonemes, vowels, schwa, liaison, syllables, prosody and accent variation.

sections.heading: Phonemes and features
sections.text: Phonology studies phonemes, the contrastive sound units of a language. French consonants include /p b t d k ɡ f v s z ʃ ʒ m n ɲ ŋ l ʁ/, with /ŋ/ mainly in loans such as parking. The glides /j ɥ w/ pattern with vowels. Distinctive features are the properties that separate phonemes: /p/ and /b/ differ by voicing, whether the vocal folds vibrate; /i/ and /y/ by rounding; /e/ and /ɛ/ by aperture, or mouth openness. A feature is distinctive only if it changes meaning, as in pas /pa/ and bas /ba/.

sections.heading: Vowels and schwa
sections.text: French has oral vowels /i y u e ø o ɛ œ ɔ a/ and nasal /ɛ̃ ɑ̃ ɔ̃ œ̃/. The front rounded /y ø œ œ̃/ are made with rounded lips and a front tongue position. /ɑ/ is marginal and often merged with /a/. Schwa /ə/ is the unstable vowel in petit /pəti/: it may be pronounced or dropped, depending on style, speed and surrounding consonants. Elision removes it before a vowel, as in le + ami → l’ami /la.mi/.

sections.heading: Liaison and syllables
sections.text: Liaison pronounces a normally silent final consonant before a vowel in the same rhythmic group: les amis /le.za.mi/. It is obligatory in some contexts, optional in others and forbidden after et. Enchaînement links an already pronounced consonant to a following vowel: avec elle /a.vɛ.kɛl/. Both can reshape syllable boundaries. French syllables prefer a consonant onset, and word stress is not lexical: the final syllable of a rhythmic group carries the main accent.

sections.heading: Accents and transcription
sections.text: Broad transcription /.../ records phonemes; narrow transcription [...] records detail. In practice, transcribe a short phrase, mark liaison and check nasal vowels. Regional and social accents vary in vowels, /ʁ/ and liaison. Southern French often keeps final schwa and has different vowel qualities; Parisian speech may drop schwa and simplify clusters. Record what a speaker says, not an ideal norm, and state the variety.

keyPoints: French consonants include /p b t d k ɡ f v s z ʃ ʒ m n ɲ ŋ l ʁ/, with /ŋ/ marginal.
French oral vowels are /i y u e ø o ɛ œ ɔ a/ and nasal vowels are /ɛ̃ ɑ̃ ɔ̃ œ̃/.
Schwa /ə/ is unstable: it may be pronounced, dropped or elided.
Liaison adds a latent consonant before a vowel; enchaînement links an already pronounced consonant.
French word stress is not lexical; the final syllable of a rhythmic group carries the main accent.
Use broad /.../ and narrow [...] transcription, and state the regional or social variety.

en.title: Morphology and Lexicology of French: Inflection, Derivation and the Lexicon
en.short: French inflection, derivation, compounding, borrowing, abbreviation and semantic change, with dictionaries and corpora.

sections.heading: Inflection and verbs
sections.text: Inflection adds grammatical information to a lexeme, a dictionary word, without making a new one. In French, finite verbs agree with their subject in person and number and carry tense and mood. A regular -er verb such as parler has a stem parl- and present-tense endings: je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent. Irregular verbs may use different stems, so the paradigm, the full set of forms, is learned form by form. Participles can agree in gender and number when used adjectivally or with certain auxiliaries.

sections.heading: Gender and number
sections.text: Nouns and adjectives carry gender and number. Gender is often lexical rather than marked by a regular ending: la table is feminine, le livre is masculine. Number is usually written with -s or -x, but many endings are not heard. Adjectives show agreement: petit, petite, petits, petites. Inflection here is agreement, not derivation: it does not create a new lexeme.

sections.heading: Derivation and compounding
sections.text: Derivation uses affixes (prefixes and suffixes) to form new lexemes. A prefix usually changes meaning (possible, impossible); a suffix can change word class (laver, lavage; rapide, rapidement). A word formation rule states which bases an affix can attach to and what category results. Compounding joins existing words or stems: porte-monnaie, chemin de fer, rouge-gorge. The compound’s meaning may not be predictable from its parts. Dictionaries record established formations; corpora, collections of texts, show which are frequent and productive.

sections.heading: Borrowing and change
sections.text: Borrowing takes words from other languages, often with adaptation: le week-end and le football from English. Abbreviation shortens existing words or phrases: professeur becomes prof; TGV stands for train à grande vitesse. Semantic change alters meaning without changing form: souris, originally the animal, also names a computer mouse by metaphor. Lexicology studies these processes together, using dictionaries for history and corpora for current usage.

keyPoints: Inflection marks grammatical categories such as person, number, gender, tense and mood without creating new lexemes.
French verb paradigms combine a stem with endings, but irregular verbs must be learned form by form.
Gender is often lexical in French, while number is usually written with -s or -x and adjectives agree.
Derivation uses prefixes and suffixes under word formation rules to create new lexemes, sometimes changing word class.
Compounding, borrowing, abbreviation and semantic change also enlarge the lexicon, the stock of words of a language.
Dictionaries record established words and their history, while corpora show frequency and current use.

en.title: Semantics and Pragmatics of French
en.short: Sense and reference, lexical relations, deixis, tense and aspect, speech acts, implicature and tu/vous politeness.

sections.heading: Meaning, sense and reference
sections.text: Semantics studies meaning in the language system; pragmatics studies meaning in use. A word’s sense is its place in a network of contrasts: “chaise” contrasts with “fauteuil”. Its reference is what it points to in the world. The phrases “l’étoile du matin” and “l’étoile du soir” can refer to the same planet, Venus, but they present it through different senses.

sections.heading: Lexical relations and ambiguity
sections.text: Synonymy is sameness or near-sameness of meaning; exact synonyms are rare. “Voiture” and “auto” are close, but “auto” is more informal. Antonymy is oppositeness: “chaud” and “froid” are gradable, while “vivant” and “mort” are complementary. Hyponymy is inclusion: “chaise” and “fauteuil” are hyponyms of “siège”, their hypernym. Polysemy is one word with related senses, as “bureau” means desk or office. Ambiguity arises when context does not settle the sense; “livre” can mean book or pound, though gender and situation usually decide.

sections.heading: Deixis, tense and aspect
sections.text: Deixis is meaning that depends on context: “je”, “ici”, “maintenant”, “demain”. Tense places an event in time; aspect shows how it is viewed. In French, “Il a lu le journal” presents a completed act, while “Il lisait” presents it as ongoing or habitual. “Quand je suis arrivé, il lisait” means that the reading was in progress when I arrived.

sections.heading: Speech acts and politeness
sections.text: Speech act theory, associated with Austin and Searle, says utterances do things: they request, promise, apologise or assert. “Pouvez-vous fermer la porte ?” is formally a question about ability, but normally a request. Grice’s implicature is meaning suggested beyond the literal words: “Il fait froid ici” may imply “close the window”. Politeness often uses indirect forms and protects face, the public self-image. French tu and vous mark solidarity or distance; usage varies by region, age and setting, so learners should observe local norms. Routines such as “Bonjour”, “Merci” and “S’il vous plaît” are socially expected in many contexts.

keyPoints: Semantics concerns conventional meaning; pragmatics concerns meaning in context.
Sense is a word’s place in a language network; reference is what it points to.
Synonymy, antonymy and hyponymy are lexical relations; polysemy and ambiguity depend on context.
Deixis depends on context, and French tense and aspect shape how events are viewed.
Speech act theory treats utterances as actions, and implicature is suggested meaning.
Tu and vous signal solidarity or distance, but their use varies by region and setting.

en.title: Sociolinguistics of French and the Francophone World
en.short: French variation, standard norms, registers, contact, and language policy across the Francophone world.

sections.heading: Variation and norms
sections.text: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies with region, social class, age and setting. French varies regionally: Quebec, Acadian, Belgian, Swiss and African varieties differ in accent, vocabulary and idiom. Social and age differences appear in pronunciation and grammar. Setting matters: formal writing favours standard forms, while conversation allows "je sais pas" for "je ne sais pas". Standard French is an idealised norm linked to education, publishing and public life. Beliefs about correctness and "pure" French are strong; the Académie française, founded in 1635, issues recommendations, but usage changes through speakers. Accents are not errors.

sections.heading: Registers and styles
sections.text: Register is a variety suited to a situation; style is a speaker’s choice within it. Courses often name soutenu (formal), courant (neutral) and familier (informal). "Je ne sais pas" is formal or neutral; "Je sais pas" is common in speech. The tu/vous choice marks solidarity or distance and can change within a conversation. Speakers accommodate to listeners, mixing forms.

sections.heading: Contact and switching
sections.text: Language contact occurs when speakers of different languages interact. Borrowing takes a word into another language and makes it part of its system: English "week-end" in French, or French "savoir-faire" in English. Code-switching is moving between languages within a conversation or sentence. A speaker in Dakar may use Wolof at the market and French at the office, and switch between them with bilingual friends. Both are normal.

sections.heading: Status and policy
sections.text: French is official in France and in many states, but its functions differ. In Senegal, French is official while Wolof is a major lingua franca. In Côte d’Ivoire, French is official amid many local languages. In Canada, English and French are federal official languages; Quebec’s Charter of the French Language (1977) promotes French. In Haiti, French and Haitian Creole are official. In the French Caribbean departments, French is official and Creole is widely spoken. Language policy decides which languages are used in schools, courts and administration; it can widen access or exclude speakers.

keyPoints: French varies by region, social class, age and setting, and regional accents are not errors.
Standard French is an idealised norm tied to education and publishing, not the only valid French.
Register concerns formality (soutenu, courant, familier), while style is a speaker’s choice within it.
Borrowing adds words to a language, and code-switching moves between languages in conversation.
French is official in France and Senegal, co-official in Canada and Haiti, and promoted in Quebec.
Language policy decides which languages are used in schools, courts and administration, affecting access.

en.title: History of the French Language
en.short: Latin to modern French: sound changes, spelling traces, standardisation, schooling and global spread.

sections.heading: From Latin to French
sections.text:
French descends from the spoken Latin of Roman Gaul, often called Vulgar Latin, not from literary Latin. As Roman rule ended, regional speech became Gallo-Romance, the Latin-based speech of Gaul, and then Old French, from about the ninth to thirteenth century. Middle French follows, covering roughly the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, and modern French is usually dated from the seventeenth century.

Sound changes left traces in spelling. In inherited words, Latin c before a became ch: cantare gives chanter, caballum gives cheval. Latin c before e or i became the sound of s: centum gives cent. Latin g before a became j: gamba gives jambe. Intervocalic consonants weakened or vanished: vita gives vie, ripa gives rive. Vowel plus nasal consonant became a nasal vowel, but n or m stays written: bon, enfant. Final consonants often fell silent but remain: petit, grand, temps. The circumflex often marks a lost s: fenestra gives fenêtre, hospitalem gives hôpital.

sections.heading: A written standard
sections.text:
Old French manuscripts vary by region. The speech of Paris and the royal court slowly gained prestige, and the royal chancery helped fix legal formulas. In 1539 the Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts, issued by Francis I, required French rather than Latin in royal legal acts. It did not make all France speak one French overnight.

Printing, from the later fifteenth century, encouraged uniform spelling and punctuation. The Académie française, founded in 1635 by Cardinal Richelieu, was given the task of standardising the language. Its dictionary first appeared in 1694. Its decisions have prestige but no legal force; usage and schools matter more.

sections.heading: Schooling and spread
sections.text: In France, the Jules Ferry laws of 1881 and 1882 made primary education free, compulsory and secular. Schools taught standard French and often discouraged regional languages. France’s colonial expansion from the seventeenth century carried French to Canada, the Caribbean, the Indian Ocean, Africa and Southeast Asia. After independence, many states kept French as an official or second language. The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie gives a current picture, but speaker numbers change, so check its latest report.

keyPoints: French descends from spoken Latin in Gaul, through Gallo-Romance and Old French to Middle and modern French.
Sound changes such as Latin c before a becoming ch and before e or i becoming s are visible in pairs like cantare/chanter and centum/cent.
Silent final consonants and the circumflex often preserve traces of older sounds, as in petit, grand, fenêtre and hôpital.
The Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (1539) required French in royal legal acts, and the Académie française (1635) promoted a standard without legal force.
Printing and, in France, the Jules Ferry laws of 1881-1882 helped spread a uniform written and schooled French.
Colonial expansion and post-independence language policy carried French to the Americas, Africa, the Indian Ocean and elsewhere; current numbers should be checked.

en.title: Reading Literature: Genres, Devices and Explication de texte
en.short: Genres, narrative voice, versification, figures of style, and the explication de texte and commentaire composé.

sections.heading: Genres and voice
sections.text: A genre is a recognised kind of writing: poetry, drama, narrative prose such as the roman (novel), nouvelle (short story) and conte (tale), and the essay. Each genre has conventions of length, form and address. Narrative voice is the teller created by the text, not the author. Point of view, or focalisation in Gérard Genette’s term, describes what the narrator knows: zero focalisation (omniscient), internal focalisation (through one character), external focalisation (only observable facts). First-person narration uses je; third-person narration uses il or elle.

sections.heading: Metre and figures
sections.text: Versification studies metre, rhyme, rhythm and stanza. French counts syllables, not stress; an alexandrin has twelve syllables. A figure of style is a deliberate turn of expression. Comparison links two things with comme or tel: Il court comme un lièvre. Metaphor identifies them without a link: Cet homme est un lion. Metonymy names a thing by something associated with it: boire un verre. Hyperbole exaggerates: Je meurs de faim. Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses: Paris est ma joie, Paris est ma peine, Paris est ma vie.

sections.heading: Explication de texte
sections.text: The explication de texte is a close, ordered reading. Read the short poem or prose extract aloud, identify its nature and situate it briefly, then analyse it in order: vocabulary, syntax, sounds, rhythm, figures, tone. Link each observation to meaning. Do not paraphrase. For example, in the invented sentence La ville dormait. Ses yeux, deux fenêtres allumées, veillaient, the metaphor yeux = fenêtres and the personification of the city create a watchful night scene. The conclusion sums up the effect.

sections.heading: Commentaire composé
sections.text: The commentaire composé is organised by themes or axes, not line by line. After a short introduction, two or three developed parts each make a claim and support it with quotations and analysis. The conclusion states the overall interest of the text. Choose axes that the passage supports; avoid biography unless it illuminates the words.

keyPoints: A genre is a recognised kind of writing with its own conventions.
Narrative voice is the teller in the text; focalisation describes what that teller knows.
French verse counts syllables; an alexandrin has twelve.
Comparison uses a link such as comme; metaphor identifies without one.
Metonymy replaces a word by an associated term; hyperbole exaggerates; anaphora repeats at the start of clauses.
Explication de texte follows the text closely; commentaire composé is organised by thematic axes.

en.title: French Literature of the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries
en.short: Theatre, moralist prose, the early novel, Enlightenment writers and the Anciens/Modernes quarrel.

sections.heading: Theatre and classicism
sections.text: Seventeenth-century French theatre moved from Baroque variety, with its ornate language and loose structure, towards classicism: order, clarity, verisimilitude (the appearance of truth) and imitation of ancient models. Corneille’s tragedies, notably Le Cid (1637), centre on heroic duty and honour. Racine’s tragedies, such as Phèdre (1677), analyse passion and guilt with great economy. Molière’s comedies, including Tartuffe (first performed 1664), satirise hypocrisy and social pretension. The classical rules were debated rather than simply imposed.

sections.heading: Moralists and the novel
sections.text: The moralists wrote short, sharp observations on human self-interest and weakness. La Rochefoucauld’s Maximes (1665) are aphorisms, brief pointed statements, often tracing virtue to vanity. Pascal’s Pensées, published after his death in 1670, are fragments for a Christian defence of faith; they are not a formal essay. Madame de La Fayette’s La Princesse de Clèves (1678) is an early psychological novel. Its heroine, married and tempted by love, chooses duty; the interest lies in inward conflict, not adventure.

sections.heading: Enlightenment prose
sections.text: Enlightenment writing valued reason, criticism, tolerance and useful knowledge. Voltaire used the conte philosophique, a short philosophical tale, in Candide (1759) to attack optimism and cruelty. Rousseau’s La Nouvelle Héloïse (1761) is a novel in letters; Émile (1762) is a treatise on education, and Du contrat social (1762) on political legitimacy. Diderot wrote fiction, art criticism and dialogue. The essay, a short prose reflection, became a flexible form for argument and satire.

sections.heading: Quarrel and Encyclopédie
sections.text: The Querelle des Anciens et des Modernes was a late seventeenth-century dispute over whether ancient writers were superior models. The Anciens defended imitation of Greece and Rome; the Moderns, including Charles Perrault, argued that their own age could surpass them. The Encyclopédie, edited by Diderot and d’Alembert from 1751, gathered knowledge and criticised inherited authority. Its volumes were censored, showing how literature and ideas could be public and dangerous.

keyPoints: Classicism prized order, clarity, verisimilitude and imitation of ancient models.
Corneille, Racine and Molière shaped seventeenth-century tragedy and comedy.
La Rochefoucauld’s Maximes and Pascal’s Pensées are moralist prose, not formal essays.
Madame de La Fayette’s La Princesse de Clèves is an early psychological novel.
Voltaire, Rousseau and Diderot used fiction, essays and dialogue to debate Enlightenment ideas.
The Querelle des Anciens et des Modernes and the Encyclopédie show disputes over authority and knowledge.

en.title: French Literature of the Nineteenth Century
en.short: Romanticism, realism, naturalism, Parnassian and symbolist poetry, and the literary press in France.

sections.heading: Romanticism and the press
sections.text:
Romanticism valued feeling, imagination, nature and national history. Chateaubriand’s Génie du christianisme (1802) and its René helped prepare French Romanticism. Hugo’s preface to Cromwell (1827) was a manifesto for new drama; his Hernani (1830) caused a theatrical battle. Hugo later opposed Napoleon III and wrote Les Châtiments (1853) in exile.

From the 1830s, newspapers such as La Presse serialised novels as roman-feuilleton. The literary press widened readership and tied writing to market and politics.

sections.heading: Realism and the novel
sections.text: Realism observes ordinary life closely and avoids idealisation. Stendhal’s Le Rouge et le Noir (1830) follows Julien Sorel through class and the Church. Balzac’s La Comédie humaine is a novel cycle offered as a social history; in Le Père Goriot (1835), money and ambition reshape family love. Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1857), tried for offence to morals and acquitted, became a model of careful realist style. Realism was a practice, not one manifesto.

sections.heading: Naturalism and Maupassant
sections.text:
Naturalism extended realism with a scientific claim. Zola’s Le Roman expérimental (1880) argued that the novelist should observe and experiment like a doctor. His Les Rougon-Macquart, a twenty-novel cycle, traces one family under the Second Empire through heredity and environment. Zola’s J’accuse (1898) defended Dreyfus and attacked the army.

Maupassant, linked to naturalism after Boule de Suif (1880), observed social types with detached irony. His stories show clerks, peasants and the pressures of the commercial press.

sections.heading: Parnassian and symbolist poetry
sections.text:
Parnassian poetry, named after Le Parnasse contemporain (from 1866), prized rhyme, technical perfection and impassive description, and it supported art for art’s sake. Symbolism, announced by Jean Moréas in 1886, reacted against it: poetry should suggest, not name, through symbols, music and correspondences.

Baudelaire’s Les Fleurs du mal (1857) made the modern city a subject and prepared symbolism. Verlaine’s 'Art poétique' puts music first. Rimbaud’s 'Lettre du voyant' (1871) makes the poet a seer. Mallarmé pursues suggestion and silence.

keyPoints: Romanticism centred on feeling, imagination and history; Hugo’s Cromwell preface (1827) was its dramatic manifesto.
Realism, practised by Stendhal, Balzac and Flaubert, observed ordinary life closely without a single manifesto.
Naturalism, defined by Zola, added a scientific claim about heredity and environment; Maupassant is often linked to it.
Parnassian poetry prized formal perfection and art for art’s sake; symbolism, announced in 1886, favoured suggestion and music.
Baudelaire, Verlaine, Rimbaud and Mallarmé reshaped poetry towards symbol and suggestion.
The roman-feuilleton in the commercial press widened readership and tied literature to market and politics.

en.title: French Literature of the Twentieth and Twenty-First Centuries
en.short: Proust to Perec and beyond: narrative experiment, surrealism, existentialism, absurd theatre and commitment.

sections.heading: Proust and Gide
sections.text:
Marcel Proust’s À la recherche du temps perdu (1913-1927) makes memory and time the substance of narrative. Involuntary memory, a sudden recollection triggered by a sensation, recovers the past. Long sentences replace plot.

André Gide’s Les Faux-Monnayeurs (1925) uses several narrators and a writer composing a novel, so the book examines its own making. Both turn the novel inward, toward consciousness and craft.

sections.heading: Surrealism and commitment
sections.text:
Guillaume Apollinaire’s Calligrammes (1918) arranges words as pictures. André Breton’s Manifeste du surréalisme (1924) defines surrealism as thought freed from reason, using automatic writing and dreams.

After 1945 Jean-Paul Sartre urged commitment, or littérature engagée: writing should address social and political responsibility. Albert Camus shared the absurd, the demand for meaning in an indifferent world, but rejected Sartre’s system. L’Étranger (1942) and Le Mythe de Sisyphe (1942) are central.

sections.heading: Absurd and nouveau roman
sections.text:
Samuel Beckett’s En attendant Godot (1952) reduces plot to waiting and talk; theatre of the absurd names plays that expose language’s failure. The nouveau roman rejected plot, character and omniscient narration. Nathalie Sarraute’s Tropismes (1939) records tiny inner movements; Marguerite Duras uses sparse dialogue and silence.

Georges Perec makes experiment a rule. La Disparition (1969) is a lipogram, a text avoiding one letter: it never uses e. The constraint forces invention and makes readers aware of language.

sections.heading: Contemporary writing
sections.text:
Later writers test the author’s place. Annie Ernaux (Nobel Prize in Literature 2022) blends autobiography with social observation; Patrick Modiano (Nobel 2014) returns to memory and uncertain identity. Michel Houellebecq writes controversial social satire. Autofiction presents the self as both lived and invented.

Twenty-first-century writing mixes documentary, history and personal voice. The author becomes a constructed presence, questioned by form and readers. Commitment changes rather than ends: from political programme to memory, testimony and identity.

keyPoints: Proust makes memory and time the substance of narrative; Gide exposes the novel’s construction.
Surrealism, defined by Breton in 1924, sought a reality beyond reason through automatic writing and dreams.
Sartre’s littérature engagée made writing a political and social responsibility; Camus explored the absurd without adopting Sartre’s system.
Beckett’s theatre of the absurd and the nouveau roman reduced plot and character to expose language and perception.
Perec’s La Disparition is a lipogram that avoids the letter e, showing how constraint can generate narrative.
Later writers such as Ernaux and Modiano mix autobiography, memory and history, making the author a constructed presence rather than a secure authority.

en.title: Francophone African Literature: Writing in French from Africa and its diaspora
en.short: Négritude, the Francophone African novel, theatre, poetry and postcolonial themes.

sections.heading: Négritude and poetry
sections.text: Négritude was a literary and cultural movement begun in the 1930s by Black students in Paris. It affirmed the value of Black cultures and rejected the idea that French culture should replace them. Its best-known figures are Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, Aimé Césaire of Martinique and Léon-Gontran Damas of French Guiana. Césaire and Damas came from the Caribbean and South America rather than sub-Saharan Africa, but the movement shaped writing across French-speaking Africa. Poetry was central: Senghor’s Chants d’ombre and Césaire’s Cahier d’un retour au pays natal mix memory with protest. Later poets such as David Diop attacked colonial rule more directly.

sections.heading: The African novel
sections.text: Camara Laye’s L’Enfant noir (1953) is a coming-of-age novel about a Guinean childhood, family craft and French schooling. Ousmane Sembène’s Les Bouts de bois de Dieu (1960) follows a railway strike and shows workers organising across colonial boundaries. Mongo Beti’s Le Pauvre Christ de Bomba (1956) satirises mission Christianity in Cameroon. Ahmadou Kourouma’s Les Soleils des indépendances (1968) exposes disillusion after independence and bends French towards Malinké, his mother tongue. Mariama Bâ’s Une si longue lettre (1979) is an epistolary novel, told in letters, about a Senegalese widow, polygamy and women’s education.

sections.heading: Theatre and themes
sections.text: Francophone African theatre draws on oral performance, proverbs and audience participation. Bernard Dadié of Côte d’Ivoire wrote satirical plays about power, and Sony Labou Tansi of the Republic of Congo criticised authoritarian rule. Common themes are colonisation and assimilation, the conflict between tradition and modernity, migration to Europe or to cities, and the failures of the postcolonial state. Assimilation was the French colonial policy of making colonised people French in language and culture, though rights were unequal. A seminar in Accra comparing L’Enfant noir and Une si longue lettre can show two views of schooling: nostalgic memory in Laye, new conflicts for women in Bâ.

keyPoints: Négritude was a 1930s movement affirming Black cultures and rejecting colonial assimilation.
Senghor, Césaire and Damas are central figures, though Césaire and Damas came from Martinique and French Guiana, not sub-Saharan Africa.
Camara Laye, Sembène, Beti, Kourouma and Bâ represent major stages of the Francophone African novel.
Kourouma’s Les Soleils des indépendances treats postcolonial disillusion, and Bâ’s Une si longue lettre treats women’s lives.
Francophone African theatre uses oral performance and often criticises power.
Recurring themes are colonisation, tradition and modernity, migration and the postcolonial state.

en.title: Francophone Caribbean and Maghrebian Literature
en.short: Antillanité, créolité, Haitian fiction, and Algerian and Moroccan writing in French.

sections.heading: Caribbean frameworks
sections.text: Caribbean writing in French comes from Martinique, Guadeloupe, Haiti and French Guiana. Antillanité is a term linked to the Martinican writer Édouard Glissant. It treats Caribbean identity as shaped by the plantation, by history and by relation with others, not by a single African origin or by French assimilation. Créolité, set out by Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant in Éloge de la créolité (1989), stresses Creole languages, mixture and plurality. Glissant later developed a poetics of Relation, arguing that cultures change through contact and that people may keep their opacity.

sections.heading: Caribbean novels
sections.text: The Haitian novel has a strong tradition of rural life, dictatorship, memory and diaspora; Jacques Roumain is a major early twentieth-century voice. Maryse Condé, from Guadeloupe, writes across the Caribbean, Africa and the United States, and questions fixed identity. Patrick Chamoiseau’s Texaco (1992) is a concrete case: a Martinican novel that gives voice to a woman remembering a shantytown and the long colonial past, mixing French with Creole oral forms.

sections.heading: Maghrebian writing
sections.text: Algerian and Moroccan fiction in French grew from colonial schooling, anti-colonial struggle and independence. Kateb Yacine’s Nedjma (1956) is a circular, fragmented novel in which Algeria and a woman named Nedjma are both desired and elusive. Assia Djebar’s L’Amour, la fantasia (1985) blends history, autobiography and women’s voices. Tahar Ben Jelloun’s La Nuit sacrée (1987) explores gender, identity and storytelling in Morocco.

sections.heading: Themes and method
sections.text: Exile appears as migration to France, return, or inner displacement. Memory carries slavery, plantation society, colonization, war and dictatorship. Language is a theme as well as a medium: writers ask whether French can carry Creole, Arabic or Berber experience. Identity is often plural and changing. When reading, ask who speaks, which languages are present, what history is remembered, and what the text leaves opaque.

keyPoints: Antillanité, linked to Glissant, sees Caribbean identity as historical and relational.
Créolité, by Bernabé, Chamoiseau and Confiant, stresses Creole languages and mixture.
The Haitian novel often treats rural life, dictatorship, memory and diaspora.
Kateb Yacine’s Nedjma and Assia Djebar’s L’Amour, la fantasia are key Algerian works of memory and identity.
Tahar Ben Jelloun’s fiction explores gender, identity and storytelling in Morocco.
Across both regions, exile, memory, language and identity are central themes.

en.title: French Civilisation and Institutions
en.short: France’s Constitution, president, parliament, local government, schools, welfare, laïcité, media and EU.

sections.heading: Constitution and executive
sections.text: The Constitution of the Fifth Republic was adopted in 1958 and approved by referendum. It created a hybrid, often called semi-presidential, system. The directly elected president appoints the prime minister, may dissolve the National Assembly and can call referendums. The government, led by the prime minister, is responsible to the National Assembly. Cohabitation, when president and parliamentary majority belong to opposite camps, has occurred. Term lengths and powers have changed; check current official sources.

sections.heading: Parliament and local government
sections.text: Parliament has two houses. The National Assembly is directly elected and can censure the government. The Senate is elected indirectly by local representatives and reviews legislation. Local government has three main tiers: regions, departments and communes. Since the decentralisation laws of the early 1980s, elected councils and mayors have held more powers. The number of regions and communes changes, so use current official figures.

sections.heading: Education and welfare
sections.text: Education is mainly centralised under the Ministry of National Education. Schooling is compulsory from age three to sixteen, but ages can change, so check the current rule. The baccalauréat is the school-leaving qualification. The Sécurité sociale, the core of the French welfare state, was created in 1945. It covers health, pensions and family benefits; unemployment insurance is separate. Social protection is financed by contributions and taxes.

sections.heading: Laïcité, media and Europe
sections.text: Laïcité is the French principle of state neutrality in religion and freedom of belief. The 1905 law separated churches and the state, with exceptions in Alsace-Moselle. A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols in state schools. Public media include France Télévisions and Radio France; ARCOM regulates broadcasting. France is a founding member of the European Communities, now the European Union, and uses the euro. EU law binds member states, though national institutions keep many powers.

keyPoints: The Fifth Republic Constitution dates from 1958 and created a semi-presidential system.
The president appoints the prime minister, but the government is responsible to the National Assembly.
Parliament has a directly elected National Assembly and an indirectly elected Senate.
Local government has regions, departments and communes, strengthened by decentralisation from the early 1980s.
The Sécurité sociale, the core of the welfare state since 1945, covers health, pensions and family benefits; unemployment insurance is separate.
Laïcité means state neutrality in religion; the 1905 law and the 2004 school law are key markers, and France is a founding EU member using the euro.

en.title: Society and Culture in Francophone Africa
en.short: Colonial legacies, language, education, cities, religion, music, film and identity debates in French-speaking Africa.

sections.heading: Colonial foundations
sections.text: Francophone Africa is a loose term for states where French has official or public roles. Many were in French West Africa or French Equatorial Africa; others were Belgian, German, Spanish or League of Nations territories, or French territories outside these federations, such as Madagascar. Colonial administrations, schools and courts used French and trained a small elite. After independence most states kept French as an official language because it was the language of administration and no single national language was accepted by all. Institutions differ: Senegal has a strong presidency; Cameroon is bilingual in French and English, and its Anglophone regions have complained of marginalisation.

sections.heading: Language and schooling
sections.text: French is rarely the first language of most citizens. Daily life uses Wolof, Bambara, Dioula, Lingala, Swahili, Kikongo, Fulfulde and many others. French dominates formal administration, higher education and some media, while national languages carry markets, family life and popular culture. In education, French is the medium in many schools, but several countries have taught in national languages in early primary or adult literacy, adding French later; policy and results vary. Access expanded after independence, yet crowded classrooms, scarce books and the gap between school French and home language remain problems.

sections.heading: Cities, faith and arts
sections.text: Urbanisation has made Dakar, Abidjan, Douala, Kinshasa and Ouagadougou centres of mixing. Young people move between French, national languages and urban slang. Religion is public and plural: Islam is strong in Senegal, Mali and Niger; Christianity in parts of Central Africa and coastal West; traditional beliefs persist alongside both. Music and film carry social debate. Senegal’s mbalax, linked to Youssou N’Dour, sets Wolof lyrics to dance rhythms; Côte d’Ivoire’s coupé-décalé and Congolese rumba are popular across borders. Cinema includes Ousmane Sembène’s films and FESPACO, the pan-African film festival in Ouagadougou.

sections.heading: Identity debates
sections.text: Language debates concern power. French links users to the wider francophone world and jobs, but critics call it an elite legacy. Rwanda has strengthened English while French remains official; Senegal promotes Wolof alongside official French. Policies vary and change, so check current law.

keyPoints: French is official in many West and Central African states, but it is rarely the first language of most citizens.
Colonial administrations used French in schools, courts and offices and trained a small elite, whose institutions often survived independence.
Education in French can widen access while also creating a gap between school language and home language.
Urban life, religion, music and film are important spaces where French and national languages mix.
Language policy debates weigh access to jobs and wider communication against identity, cost and colonial history.
Countries differ: Senegal, Cameroon and Rwanda show different paths, and current laws should be checked.

en.title: Translation Theory and Practice: French and English
en.short: Approaches to French-English translation, practical problems, and the translator’s choices and ethics.

sections.heading: Approaches
sections.text:
Translation is rewriting a text for readers of another language. Literal translation follows the words and syntax of the source; free translation gives the sense in natural target language. Literal work can preserve form but may break English or French grammar. Free work reads well but can drift from the source.

Equivalence means matching meaning, function or effect rather than words. Nida distinguished formal equivalence, which keeps form and content, from dynamic equivalence, which aims at a similar response in the target reader. Skopos theory, from Vermeer, says the purpose of the translation guides the choices. Venuti described domestication, which makes the text feel familiar, and foreignisation, which keeps source culture visible.

sections.heading: Practical problems
sections.text:
Register is the level of formality. French tu and vous, and English you, rarely match neatly. Idioms and fixed expressions resist word-for-word work: Il fait un froid de canard means literally 'it makes a cold of duck', but naturally 'it is freezing'. False friends mislead: actuellement means currently, not actually, so 'Actuellement, il travaille à Paris’ is 'Currently, he is working in Paris'.

Culture-specific terms such as préfecture may need a short gloss, because English has no exact equivalent. Non-standard French, including slang, regional speech and verlan, a syllable-reversal slang, needs a target voice that is equally marked, not flat standard English. Check choices against context and the whole text.

sections.heading: Choices and ethics
sections.text:
The translator decides what to keep, explain, adapt or omit, and should justify each decision. Accuracy comes first: do not invent facts, dates or names, and do not silently drop difficult material. Keep the author’s tone and intention. Explain culture-specific terms briefly when needed. Respect confidentiality and credit sources.

A useful method is to draft, compare source and target sentence by sentence, then revise for natural language. Ask a reader to check meaning and register. Where two versions are possible, choose the one that serves the purpose and the reader, and say what you did.

keyPoints: Literal translation follows words; free translation follows sense, and neither is always right.
Equivalence aims at the same meaning or effect, not word-for-word matching.
Skopos theory says the purpose of the translation guides the strategy.
Domestication brings the text close to the target reader; foreignisation keeps source culture visible.
False friends and idioms show why word-for-word translation often fails.
Ethical translators do not invent, hide omissions, or erase culture-specific meaning without explanation.

en.title: Teaching French as a Foreign Language
en.short: Methods, the four skills, planning, CEFR levels, testing and French in school systems.

sections.heading: Methods in FLE
sections.text: Didactique du FLE is the study of teaching French as a foreign language, that is, French learned where it is not the main language of daily life. The grammar-translation method taught rules and word lists through translation. The direct method used only French. Audio-lingual teaching drilled patterns. Communicative language teaching (CLT) centres lessons on real meaning. Task-based teaching (TBLT) asks learners to complete a task, such as planning a market visit, then reviews the language used. Teachers often combine methods.

sections.heading: Skills and planning
sections.text:
Listening and speaking are taught with short recordings, clear models and pair work. Reading uses pre-reading questions, skimming and scanning. Writing moves from controlled sentences to short paragraphs, using a model and checklist.

A lesson plan states objectives, level, stages, timing and materials. Objectives should be observable: “Learners can ask a price and understand the answer.” Materials include the textbook, pictures, audio and authentic documents such as a menu. Adapt them to the class.

sections.heading: CEFR and assessment
sections.text:
The Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) describes six levels: A1 and A2 (basic user), B1 and B2 (independent user), C1 and C2 (proficient user). It uses can-do descriptors, not a fixed syllabus.

Testing should match objectives and be valid and reliable. Use placement, formative and summative tests. Correct errors with care: an error is systematic, a mistake is a slip. Oral correction can wait until after an activity; written work can use a simple code.

sections.heading: French in schools
sections.text:
In much of Francophone Africa, French is an official or school language, so learners may study it as a second language. In Nigeria, French is usually a school subject, not an official language. In France it is the language of schooling; in many other countries it is a foreign language.

A teacher in Kano might plan a beginner lesson on market prices: pairs practise “Combien ça coûte ?”, then perform a short role-play while the teacher notes errors for later correction.

keyPoints: Didactique du FLE studies how to teach French as a foreign language, and methods have moved from grammar-translation to communicative and task-based teaching.
The four skills are listening, speaking, reading and writing; each needs focused practice, and grammar supports them.
A lesson plan states observable objectives, level, stages, timing and materials, and materials should be adapted to the class.
The CEFR describes six can-do levels from A1 to C2 and is not a fixed syllabus.
Tests should be valid and reliable, and errors should be corrected selectively, with systematic errors treated differently from slips.
French is a second or school language in much of Francophone Africa, a school subject in Nigeria, and a foreign language in many other countries.

en.title: Research Methods in French Studies
en.short: Designing a small French studies project: questions, sources, corpus, analysis, citation and ethics.

sections.heading: Choosing a question
sections.text: Start with a question that is narrow, answerable and relevant to French language, literature or civilisation. A topic names an area; a question asks something specific. Women in francophone African novels is a topic. How does a named novel present a mother’s silence? is a question.
