Write the question, then a short plan: primary material, method, likely sources and limit. Check that the project can be finished with the time and access you have. Your supervisor can help you narrow it.

sections.heading: Sources and corpus
sections.text: Use the library catalogue, your department’s reading lists and online bibliographies. For French studies, useful starting points include the Bibliothèque nationale de France catalogue and Gallica, the MLA International Bibliography, Cairn.info, Persée and Google Scholar. Distinguish primary sources, the texts or data you analyse, from secondary sources, other scholars’ work. A corpus is the set of texts or examples you analyse. Keep a reading list with full details from the start. If you use a sample, state how you chose it.

sections.heading: Analysis and citation
sections.text: Textual analysis reads closely for form, argument, imagery and context. Linguistic analysis may count features, such as pronouns, tenses or vocabulary, and compare them. For example, in 100 headlines from one Dakar online newspaper, suppose 40 contain on and 25 contain nous. That is 40 ÷ 100 = 40% and 25 ÷ 100 = 25%. Report the date range and selection rule. Cite every borrowed idea. Styles vary: MLA, Chicago and APA are common, but follow your department’s handbook exactly.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Research ethics means honesty and care. Do not plagiarise: acknowledge words, ideas and data. Quote accurately and mark omissions. Respect copyright when copying or reproducing images and long passages. If you interview people, obtain informed consent, explain the purpose, store data safely and anonymise names where promised. Keep notes and drafts. Write the long essay in clear sections: introduction, method, analysis, conclusion and bibliography. Check the final text against the question.

keyPoints: A research question should be narrow, answerable and linked to language, literature or civilisation.
Primary sources are the texts or data you analyse; secondary sources are other scholars’ work.
A corpus is a defined set of texts or examples, and its selection rule must be stated.
Textual analysis reads closely, while linguistic analysis may count and compare features.
For simple counts, a percentage is count ÷ total × 100.
Cite all borrowed ideas, follow your department’s style, and protect participants through consent and anonymity.

en.title: Advanced Linguistic Theory and Analysis
en.short: Generative syntax, semantics, constraint-based phonology, corpora and argument from French data.

sections.heading: Theory and evidence
sections.text: At master’s level, theory is judged by coverage, predictions and parsimony. Generative syntax asks what knowledge of French a speaker has and how it is represented. The Minimalist Program treats sentences as built by Merge, which combines syntactic objects, and by Agree, which matches features such as person and number. Data include grammaticality judgements and corpus attestations.

sections.heading: Syntax and semantics
sections.text: Lexical semantics studies word meaning: sense relations, argument structure and frames. Propositional semantics studies truth conditions and compositionality: the meaning of a sentence is built from its parts. Scope and presupposition matter. In French, Jean et Marie se regardent is ambiguous between a reciprocal reading (they look at each other) and a reflexive reading (each looks at herself or himself). A good analysis predicts both readings and explains how syntax and the lexicon constrain them.

sections.heading: Constraint-based phonology
sections.text: Optimality Theory (Prince and Smolensky) treats grammar as ranked constraints. Constraints are universal, but their ranking differs by language. Faithfulness constraints preserve underlying forms; markedness constraints ban marked structures. French liaison shows this: the final consonant of les surfaces as z before a vowel, as in les amis, but not before a consonant. A ranking of onset, coda and faithfulness constraints can model the pattern.

sections.heading: Corpora and argument
sections.text: Corpus methods count patterns in authentic French; computational methods tag, parse and model meaning. Frantext supports historical and literary searches, and the French Treebank supplies syntactic annotation. Frequency is not grammaticality, so corpus findings need linguistic analysis. A sustained argument states a claim, gives French data, analyses it in a framework, compares alternatives and tests predictions. Read primary articles for their question, data, analysis and limitations.

keyPoints: Generative syntax models speakers’ knowledge with operations such as Merge and Agree.
Lexical semantics studies word meaning and argument structure, while propositional semantics studies truth conditions and compositionality.
Optimality Theory explains phonological patterns through ranked faithfulness and markedness constraints.
French liaison, where a latent consonant surfaces before a vowel, is a classic case for constraint ranking.
Corpus and computational methods supply attested data and annotation, but frequency does not equal grammaticality.
A linguistics argument from French data states a claim, analyses the data, compares alternatives and tests predictions.

en.title: Literary Theory and Criticism: Reading French Texts
en.short: Major critical schools and how they read French texts, plus writing a critical essay.

sections.heading: Formalism and structure
sections.text:
Formalism studies how literary devices make a text literary. Structuralism, after Ferdinand de Saussure, treats a text as a system of signs and oppositions. Narratology, after Gérard Genette, analyses voice (who speaks), focalisation (whose perspective) and time (order, duration, frequency).

Take Baudelaire’s sonnet “Correspondances”. A formalist notes its sonnet shape and image patterns. A structuralist maps oppositions such as night and light, or fresh and corrupt scents. A narratologist asks who speaks and through whose perception the images are filtered. They sharpen close reading.

sections.heading: Unconscious and society
sections.text:
Psychoanalytic criticism reads texts for unconscious desire, repression and symptom. Freud is the start; Jacques Lacan recasts the unconscious as structured like language, so slips and gaps matter. Marxist and sociological criticism reads class, ideology, labour and social formation. Lucien Goldmann linked literary form to the worldview of social groups.

In Balzac’s Le Père Goriot, a Marxist reading traces money, inheritance and ambition across Paris. A psychoanalytic reading asks what paternal love and loss conceal. Both must quote detail, not apply labels.

sections.heading: Gender and meaning
sections.text:
Feminist and gender criticism examines how texts construct masculinity and femininity, and how canons exclude women. Simone de Beauvoir’s claim that one becomes a woman is a starting point; Hélène Cixous proposes écriture féminine, writing of the body. Deconstruction, after Jacques Derrida, shows how oppositions such as presence/absence depend on each other and undermine themselves. Reader-response theory, with Iser and Jauss, sees meaning as produced in reading and shaped by a horizon of expectations.

In Flaubert’s Madame Bovary, a feminist reading examines Emma’s constrained roles; a deconstructive reading tests the novel’s oppositions between romance and reality; a reader-response reading asks how sympathy shifts.

sections.heading: Writing the essay
sections.text: Choose a question and one or two schools, then close-read passages. State the method, analyse evidence, and show what the reading reveals that summary cannot. Compare schools where they conflict. Cite the French edition and translation you use. A good essay argues, not lists theorists.

keyPoints: Formalism studies literary devices; structuralism reads texts as sign systems; narratology analyses voice, focalisation and time.
Psychoanalytic criticism traces unconscious desire and symptom; Marxist and sociological criticism traces class, ideology and social formation.
Feminist and gender criticism examines constructed gender roles and the canon; deconstruction exposes unstable oppositions.
Reader-response theory treats meaning as produced in reading, shaped by a horizon of expectations.
Apply a school to specific passages, compare schools where they conflict, and cite the French edition and translation.
A critical essay makes an argument from close evidence, not a list of theorists.

en.title: Postcolonial Theory and Francophone Writing
en.short: Said, Spivak, Bhabha, Césaire, Fanon and Glissant; négritude, créolité, littérature-monde, language and memory.

sections.heading: Postcolonial theory
sections.text:
Postcolonial studies asks how colonial power shaped knowledge, language and identity. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) argues that Western scholarship built an image of the East as backward and exotic, serving domination.

Gayatri Spivak’s Can the Subaltern Speak? (1988) asks whether the colonised poor, the subaltern, can be heard within elite discourse; she calls the harm done to their ways of knowing epistemic violence. Homi Bhabha (1994) describes hybridity, the mixed forms colonial rule produces, and mimicry, imitation that never quite succeeds and so unsettles authority.

sections.heading: Négritude and Fanon
sections.text:
Négritude began in 1930s Paris with Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas. It affirmed black cultural values against colonial contempt. Césaire’s Cahier d’un retour au pays natal (1939) and Discours sur le colonialisme (1950) attack colonial humanism.

Frantz Fanon, in Peau noire, masques blancs (1952), saw négritude as a response to racism but argued that identity must move beyond race. Les Damnés de la terre (1961) presents decolonisation as a struggle both physical and mental.

sections.heading: Antillanité, créolité, Relation
sections.text:
Édouard Glissant’s antillanité turned from Africa to the Caribbean: the Middle Passage, plantation society and composite identity. In Poétique de la Relation (1990) he proposes Relation, contact between cultures that changes all sides, and créolisation, the unpredictable mixing that follows. He defends the right to opacity: a people need not be fully transparent to outsiders.

Créolité, proclaimed in Éloge de la créolité (1989) by Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant, celebrates Creole language and oral storytelling. Maryse Condé warned that it could harden mixture into a new orthodoxy.

sections.heading: Language, memory, migration
sections.text: The Algerian writer Kateb Yacine called French a butin de guerre, spoils taken in war. The manifesto Pour une littérature-monde en français (Le Monde, 2007) declared the end of francophone literature as a separate category; critics replied that it still measured writing by Paris. Memory and migration run through Chamoiseau’s Texaco (1992) and Sembène’s film La Noire de... (1966).

keyPoints: Said’s Orientalism shows how Western knowledge about the East was produced within, and served, colonial power.
Spivak’s subaltern and Bhabha’s hybridity and mimicry question whether colonial discourse is ever complete.
Négritude affirmed black values; Fanon saw it as a response to racism but argued for moving beyond race.
Glissant’s antillanité and Relation, and the créolité of Bernabé, Chamoiseau and Confiant, centre Caribbean mixture and Creole.
The 2007 littérature-monde manifesto rejected francophone literature as a separate category, and critics found it still Paris-centred.
Language choice, migration and memory are political questions in francophone writing and film.

en.title: Dissertation Research and Writing in French Studies
en.short: Framing a question, reviewing literature, methods, ethics, sources, structure and the viva.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A dissertation answers one clear question, not a whole subject. Start from a puzzle: something in a French text, a corpus of speech, or a practice in a Francophone country that needs explaining. Narrow it until it can be answered with the time and sources you have. Write the question as a sentence, then state the gap: what existing work has not yet shown. A hypothesis is a testable claim; a research objective states what you will do to answer the question. Supervisors expect a proposal of a few pages before writing begins.

sections.heading: Methods and sources
sections.text: The literature review shows you know the debate, not just the topic. Group studies by argument, then say where they agree, disagree and leave gaps. Use the methods of your field: close reading and textual analysis for literature; corpus or questionnaire data for linguistics; archival and interview work for area studies. Say why the method fits the question, and state its limits. Keep a searchable record of every source from day one.

sections.heading: Ethics and citation
sections.text: Ethics covers consent, anonymity and honesty. Interviews need informed consent: participants understand the purpose and may withdraw. Anonymise names unless permission is given. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, ideas or data as your own, and it applies to translation and paraphrase too. Cite every borrowed idea, use a consistent style such as MLA or APA, and check your institution’s rules, which differ by country.

sections.heading: Structure and defence
sections.text: A common shape is introduction, literature review, method, analysis chapters, conclusion, bibliography, annexes. The introduction states the question, gap, method and plan. Each chapter should make one point and link to the next. In the defence (viva), you usually present briefly, then answer questions. Expect examiners to ask why you chose this corpus and what you would do differently. Rehearse aloud, know your own evidence, and admit limits calmly.

keyPoints: A dissertation answers one narrow, stated research question, not a broad topic.
The literature review maps the debate and identifies the gap you fill.
Choose the method that fits the question: textual, corpus, archival or interview based.
Plagiarism includes uncredited paraphrase and translation, so cite every borrowed idea.
Informed consent and anonymity protect people who take part in your research.
In the viva, explain your choices and limits calmly and know your own evidence.
